questions.q: Why is a Pod, not a single container, the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?
options: A Pod can wrap one or more containers that are always scheduled together on the same node, sharing a network namespace
A Pod is just a renamed container image with no other purpose
A Pod is only used for multi-node applications, never for a single container
A Pod replaces the need for a container runtime entirely
questions.explain: A Pod wraps one or more containers that get scheduled together onto the same node and share a network namespace (and optionally volumes), which is why Kubernetes schedules at the Pod level rather than the individual container level.

questions.q: What does a ReplicaSet's reconciliation loop actually check?
options: Whether the container image tag has changed since the last deploy
Whether the number of Pods matching its label selector equals the desired replica count
Whether etcd has enough disk space for new objects
Whether the Deployment above it has been updated recently
questions.explain: A ReplicaSet only reconciles count: it compares how many Pods matching its selector currently exist against spec.replicas, creating or deleting whole Pods to close the gap. It never edits a running Pod's content.

questions.q: If you edit the container image in a bare ReplicaSet's Pod template, what happens to its already-running Pods?
options: They are automatically restarted one at a time with the new image
The ReplicaSet creates a brand-new set of Pods immediately and deletes the old ones
They keep running the old image indefinitely, since a ReplicaSet reconciles count, never content
Kubernetes refuses the edit until a Deployment is created first
questions.explain: A ReplicaSet has no mechanism to update existing Pods' content — only a Deployment manages that kind of controlled change, by creating a new ReplicaSet with the updated template.

questions.q: What does a Deployment do that a bare ReplicaSet cannot?
options: Assign Pods to specific worker nodes directly, bypassing the scheduler
Create a new ReplicaSet per template change and gradually shift replicas from the old ReplicaSet to the new one, enabling rolling updates
Store the cluster's state in place of etcd
Allow Pods to run without any label selector at all
questions.explain: A Deployment sits above the ReplicaSet layer specifically to manage change over time — it creates a new ReplicaSet whenever the Pod template changes and drives the rollout between old and new ReplicaSets.

questions.q: In `kubectl get pods --show-labels` output showing a Pod named web-app-7d9f8c6b5d-x2k9p, what does the naming pattern reveal?
options: The Pod was created directly by the Deployment with no ReplicaSet involved
The hash segment is a random Pod ID with no relation to any other object
The Pod name encodes which worker node it is scheduled on
The Pod was created by a ReplicaSet (named with the hash of its Pod template), which was itself created by a Deployment
questions.explain: The Deployment creates a ReplicaSet named after a hash of its Pod template (e.g. web-app-7d9f8c6b5d), and that ReplicaSet creates Pods named <replicaset-name>-<random-suffix> — visible directly in kubectl describe pod's Controlled By field.
